extracted.intended_audience: Congressional staff, agency rulemaking officials, GSA/OMB program managers, and other policymakers responsible for federal e-rulemaking/comment platforms
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating and specifying standards, policies, and technical/operational features for federal electronic notice-and-comment (e-rulemaking) dockets and public comment platforms (e.g., Regulations.gov, FCC ECFS). Focus is on integrity, usability, legal compliance, governance, and modernization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaningful public participation / accessibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The e-rulemaking system should provide all Americans and interested stakeholders a meaningful opportunity to participate in the regulatory development process; the filing, posting, and retrieval of comments should be as easy, inclusive, and accessible as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide 24/7 availability, user guides, short-text express comment boxes and support for longer uploads; design for human-centered usability so members of the public (including small businesses and rural residents) can find dockets, submit comments, and know their comments were received.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrity and protection against abuse (bots, fake comments, stolen identities)
rubrics_metrics.description: The platform must protect against mass-generated, fraudulent, or malicious submissions (e.g., bots, stolen identities, fake or repeated submissions) that can overwhelm dockets and distort or drown out substantive input.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples cited include comments posted under stolen identities, comments posted in the names of dead people, millions of comments from disposable email domains, coordinated submissions at the same second, and comments containing malware. Consider CAPTCHA or other human-verification tools, identity-authentication approaches, and eliminating or limiting open APIs used for mass submissions—while weighing tradeoffs and spoofing/workaround risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on substance over raw counts
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should evaluate comments based on their substantive content (significant factual, legal, and policy arguments) rather than the numeric total of submissions for or against a position.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A rulemaking is 'not a public opinion survey'; the record should show responses to significant issues raised. Even in proceedings with millions of comments, the agency must identify and respond to significant arguments and base decisions on record evidence to satisfy legal obligations under the APA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistent policies and procedures for removal/redaction of abusive or spam comments
rubrics_metrics.description: There should be consistent, government-wide guidelines for when and how abusive, profane, irrelevant, malware-laden, or identity-theft comments are removed or redacted from public dockets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Currently agencies using Regulations.gov have different approaches; inconsistency hampers integrity and public confidence. Example: only one agency (CFTC) reported flagging false-identity comments to law enforcement. GAO, IG, and Congressional recommendations should inform best practices for removal and redaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authentication & configurable attribution requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The system should support configurable agency choices about which commenter fields to require (e.g., name, address, email, citizenship) and whether to allow anonymous comments, while enabling mechanisms for verification where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some agencies require only the comment text (anonymous), others require name/address/email with variable validation. Agencies decide what commenter information is made public; any identity verification policy must balance accessibility with fraud prevention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection and stewardship of personally identifiable information (PII)
rubrics_metrics.description: Platforms must protect PII submitted to dockets and maintain appropriate custodial responsibilities, disaster recovery, continuous monitoring, and auditing for data security.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: GSA is described as custodian responsible for protecting data, but comments/data are owned by the rulemaking agency. Standards for PII protection and access control should be implemented consistently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Searchability and retrievability of comments
rubrics_metrics.description: The platform must enable users and agency staff to search, retrieve, and review comments effectively (keyword and full-text search), so substantive comments can be found and used in rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical GAO findings noted difficulties searching Regulations.gov; improvements include better search capabilities, docket home pages highlighting deadlines, and tools to surface major filings and relevant comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: System resilience, capacity, and uptime
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure sufficient network capacity, uptime, and technical resilience so the platform remains available and usable during high-volume proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FCC improved network capacity to prevent disruptions. Modernization plans should address scalability to handle spikes in large rulemakings without outages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to handle volume through automation and analytics (filtering, flagging)
rubrics_metrics.description: Because human review of every comment is impractical at scale, the system should provide automated tools and analytics to identify mass-mail campaigns, duplicates, probable bot activity, malware, and other noise for triage and agency review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Pew analysis showing many identical/repeated comments and surges of submissions at the same second. Agencies should use analytics to distinguish mass mail campaigns (which may be legitimate) from astroturfing and automated abuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance openness with anti-abuse measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Any measures to limit abuse (e.g., CAPTCHA, authentication, limiting APIs) must be designed to avoid unduly restricting legitimate public participation or excluding disadvantaged populations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legitimate advocacy organizations use mass-submission tools; removing or restricting those channels affects participation. Technologies like CAPTCHA can be spoofed; cost, accessibility, and potential exclusion must be considered in choosing solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Governance, shared service model, and funding transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: E-rulemaking should be managed as a shared service with clear governance (Executive Steering Committee, Advisory Board) and funded via interagency agreements with transparent budget processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The program is a shared service (FDMS + Regulations.gov) with ~221 partner rulemaking organizations and an average annual budget around $8 million; major decisions are subject to committee/board votes—governance affects prioritization of upgrades and policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interoperability and data integration for analytics
rubrics_metrics.description: Integrate e-rulemaking data and IT with other regulatory systems to support cross-system analytics, regulatory agendas, and better information sharing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: GSA's goals include integrating data and IT to support analytics and leveraging Regulatory Information Service Center (RISC) for Unified Regulatory Agenda coordination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Configurable agency workflows and posting processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Support agency-configurable workflows for intake, automated posting frequency, moderation processes, and the timing/delay between submission and public posting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Posting frequency varies: FCC posts every 2 hours via an automated process; other agencies differ. Agencies currently set their own posting and review procedures—platform should support those differences while promoting best practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal compliance with APA and defensibility in court
rubrics_metrics.description: The commenting system and agency response practices must enable agencies to satisfy Administrative Procedure Act requirements—providing a meaningful opportunity to comment and properly responding to significant issues so final rules are defensible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies focus on substance and addressing significant factual/legal arguments; ECFS/Regulations.gov serve as the repository for the rulemaking record used in litigation and judicial review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling of malicious content and malware
rubrics_metrics.description: Systems must detect and address malicious file submissions and malware within comments to protect public users and agency systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pew found comments containing computer viruses; leaving such comments online risks infecting users reviewing dockets. Agencies should scan and remove or quarantine malicious attachments.

rubrics_metrics.name: API and mass-submission policy management
rubrics_metrics.description: Manage and govern API access and machine-to-machine submission channels to permit legitimate mass filings while preventing abusive automated campaigns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FCC is considering eliminating an open API used for mass comments; platforms should provide alternative, controlled submission methods for advocacy groups that preserve transparency and attribution while reducing abuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support for multiple comment formats and user needs
rubrics_metrics.description: The platform should accept short express comments and longer standard comments, in most common file formats, to accommodate varied commenter needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ECFS accepts a text box for short comments and uploads in most file formats, supporting broader participation. Any modernization should maintain and extend flexible input methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human-centered design and stakeholder engagement in modernization
rubrics_metrics.description: Modernization efforts should use human-centered design, engage agencies, Congress, and the public to identify priorities, and produce a roadmap for improvements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: GSA intends to engage stakeholders and complete an initial road map for modernization (e.g., by FY2020), focusing on customer experience, analytics, and interactions with agency systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency, public confidence, and trustworthiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Platform integrity, consistent agency practices, and clear communication about how comments are used are necessary to maintain public confidence in the rulemaking process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problems such as millions of fake comments, profane or threatening comments, and identity theft diminish trust; consistency across agencies and visible anti-abuse steps will help restore confidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Auditability, monitoring, and recordkeeping
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain continuous monitoring, auditing, logging, and disaster recovery capabilities to ensure the integrity and availability of dockets and to support investigations (e.g., into fraud or abuse).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: GSA as custodian should ensure disaster recovery and continuous monitoring; audit trails support investigations and enforcement (e.g., flagging false-identity submissions for law enforcement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Promote earlier and more substantive participation (early participation mechanisms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Encourage mechanisms (e.g., advance notice for major rules) that invite earlier, substantive engagement to improve rule quality rather than late-stage mass submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative proposals like the Early Participation in Regulations Act would require advanced notice for major rules to garner earlier, more useful input—goal is not fewer comments but earlier, substantive comments.
